en: Then, in the beginning, there was sound; from that, the imperishable cause arose.
O Brahmin, those who know Brahman know that Brahman is the cause and the bestower of liberation. || 1 ||
Therefore, the God who bestows everything is known as the Mass of Sounds (Śabdarāśi);
he consists of four hundred and fifty chapters, and is the supreme essence of both the source and the seed.
The seed-syllable (bīja) consisting of sixteen letters begins with 'a' and ends with the visarga;
the remaining thirty-four letters are the womb (yoni), imperishable and composed of syllables.
That is the power of the God of gods; by it this entire world is pervaded.
It is the supreme Śaiva knowledge, subtle, which is the highest means of liberation.

Through the various distinctions of knowledge beginning with the Vedas, and through the different forms of the knowledge of Śiva, He stands here like a wish-fulfilling gem as the cause of everything. 5.
The single knowledge of Śiva is divided again tenfold;
likewise, it is further expanded into eighteen divisions through various sub-classifications.
The first of these is Kāmika; beyond that is Yogodbhava;
then Acintya, Kāraṇa, Jñāna, Ajita, and the one named Dīpta.
Likewise, they know another subtle division consisting of a thousand;
beyond that, there are ten divisions, namely Aṃśumān and Suprabha.
Therein, the first is the Vijaya, and likewise the other is the Niśvāsa;
then the Svāyambhuva, the Āgneya, the Vīrabhadra, and the Saraurava.
Then follow the Makuṭa, the Visara, and the Canrahāsa;
after that, the Mukhabimbaka, the Anyat, the Prodgīta, and the Lalita.
The Siddha, the one called Santāna, the Śārvodgīta, the Nṛsiṃhaka, the Kiraṇa, and the Pārameśvara—this is the compendium of the divisions of the Tantra. || 11 ||
Thus, this Śivajñāna is divided again in many ways;
due to its various subdivisions, there is no limit to its distinctions.

All other varieties of initiation, whether they be major or minor, serve the purpose of providing conviction and yield the fruits of both spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) and liberation (mukti). || 13 ||

Since initiation (dīkṣā) is held to be the cause for both spiritual attainment (siddhi) and liberation (mukti), and since it is desired for these two purposes, you ought to explain that which has the mantra as its primary element. || 14 ||
Thus addressed, Mahādeva, whose crest-jewel was the quivering moon,
spoke the mantras by which this entire world is pervaded.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on Emanation, in the Svāyambhuva-sūtra-saṅgraha.
